requests.title: A register item records when, and by whom, it closed
requests.answerToSource: Closed, and it was worse than you filed it. You reported an API defect; the SCREEN had the same hole — every closure made through the interface also lost its date and its closer. `raid_item` now carries `closed_on` and `closed_by`. Nothing is back-dated: a row closed before this migration is closed on a day nobody recorded, and null says exactly that rather than inventing `opened_on` or the migration's own date. `closed_by` names a person from the directory, not the account that pushed the button — the audit trail already carries the second, and what an auditor asks a year later is on whose word the risk was lifted. Your sync may send its own date and name and they are read back unchanged; send none and closing stamps today and the person behind the account. Reopening clears both, and a closure date with no closure is refused naming the gesture.
requests.observed: status: Closed answers 200 and reads back closed while closed_on stays null: the ledger's closure date is lost on every row a sync closes.

A project date now says what it rests on exactly as 040 did for a milestone (your D-057): committed, or a placeholder that is never reported late until the condition producing the real date is measured. The date stays mandatory — the engine draws, sorts and compares with it — what is added is what it is worth. The sponsor resolves in the directory rather than being free text, because on a project the sponsor is somebody you telephone and a name that does not resolve is a string, not a responsibility. And the write API now refuses a body it does not understand, naming the key, listing what is accepted, pointing at the contract and saying nothing was written — your own D-10 is the argument. That strictness is only safe because the four fields you measured were made real in the same migration. One thing we found while closing it: the AGENDA was calling a placeholder finish '42d late', which sends a steering meeting after a slip nobody promised not to have. Fixed, with a test that a committed date missed is still reported late.

requests.title: Portfolio prioritisation by value and risk against capacity: score demand and live projects on claimed value, confidence, RAID exposure and capacity consumed, ordered against available capacity
delivered: shared/prioritise.js (four inputs, stated weighting, capacity and money lines, per-programme views)

requests.measure: server/test/prioritise.test.js — describes « REQ-24 · the capacity line » (incl. « a programme's list is a filter of the group's order, not a second ranking with its own line ») and « REQ-24 · changing a weight re-ranks, and is audited »; server/test/scenarios.test.js (FX-12)

requests.answerToSource: Built, and on main since 5.16.0 (built on the 5.15.0 line, not announced in that changelog section); FX-12 added what-if weights in 5.32.0. Demand and live projects are ranked on ONE list on four inputs — claimed value, confidence (1–5, never inferred), the worst open RAID exposure and the capacity the work consumes — under a weighting the group states. Every ranked row carries its decomposition; a row missing any input is NOT placed, is listed apart and names what is missing and where to fill it. A line is drawn where the group's people (and, if one is agreed, the capital envelope) run out. Changing a weight needs a reason, asserts a row version, re-ranks at once and is audited with before and after. Two things you should know: the per-programme list is the group's order FILTERED, with the group's line, not a second ranking with its own pool, because your people are shared across programmes; and the weighting is one per group, set at group level (priority.weighting). What to try: GET /api/prioritisation on your book, fill the missing inputs of one not-placed project, then change a weight with a note and read the audit trail.

requests.title: One ladder per project: a project under a programme with a declared ladder carries exactly that ladder, and an existing book migrates onto it without duplicates
delivered: server/src/wbs.js#scaffoldProject reads the programme's ladder only
server/src/wbs.js#planLadderMove (adopt matching gates, create missing ones, retire the rest, never duplicate)
server/src/routes/ladder.js (GET /api/projects/:id/ladder dry run, POST /api/projects/:id/ladder the audited act, ladder.migrate in shared/rbac.js)
requests.measure: server/test/ladder.test.js — « l'acte : six adoptés, zéro créé, quatre retirés », « le livre relu : six barreaux, dix lignes, aucun doublon », « l'acte est idempotent », « le second passage du chargeur ne fait aucune écriture créante »
requests.observed: RT365 measured ten milestones where six were intended, and filed it as a defect rather than a preference.
requests.answerToSource:
The migration half is built, and on main since 5.16.0 (built on the 5.15.0 line). A project created under a programme with a ladder still gets exactly that ladder. An existing project now MOVES onto its programme's ladder by an explicit act: GET /api/projects/<id>/ladder is a dry run that writes nothing and names what will be adopted, created and retired, and which signed gates you must acknowledge; POST with that version does it in one audited transaction, adopting the milestones that already match, creating only the missing rungs and never duplicating. A second run writes nothing, and your loader's second run makes no creating write. What to try: on one of your sixteen RBT projects, read the dry run, then post it with the acknowledgements it asks for and count six gate milestones.

Q-7, answered from the code you asked us to read: the OPEN RISKS tile counts `status === "Open" && type === "Risk"`, scoped to the projects the filter has selected, plus portfolio-wide items that carry no project. Your withdrawal of the implication was right.

requests.title: Governance quality signals on the portfolio page: decision latency, action ageing, gate cycle time, RAID review compliance, exception age
requests.observed: A PMO that cannot see its own throughput cannot improve it, and these five are the leading indicators of a programme quietly stalling.
requests.answerToSource: Closed, at your priority and with your constraint honoured: no new data entry, no migration, five clocks read from timestamps the book already keeps. Every one of them can say 'not measured' with a reason, because five new metrics are five new places to make the REQ-33 mistake — a programme that has closed no gates does not have a cycle time of zero and is not doing well. The median leads and the tail travels with it, your own sentence about a healthy mean and a two-year tail. Gate cycle time refuses to average a four-gate and a six-gate ladder and keeps each rung's own figure instead. None of the five carries a colour: nobody has agreed what 'too slow' means for your group, and a threshold chosen in our file would be exactly the fabrication you caught us at. Three things we found while building it are filed as REQ-45, REQ-46 and REQ-47 — read those before you read the metrics, because two of the five are unmeasurable on a real book today for reasons that are governance holes, not measurement bugs.

requests.answerToSource: Closed in 5.25.0 (D-36.14). A criterion can cite a commit (`owner/repo@sha`) or a checksum (`sha256:<hex>`); the gate record shows what was cited and by whom; once the criterion is met or its gate done, changing the citation creates a new version that supersedes the old, which is kept and never edited (409). Meridian stores and shows the reference and never claims to have verified it. What to try: cite a commit on a met criterion, then change it and read both versions.

requests.title: A value dashboard for the executive: spend against case, benefits by status, overdue reviews, top risks by exposure, gates due, exceptions open
requests.observed: The portfolio view answers 'is it on time and on budget'; nobody can answer 'is it worth it'.
requests.answerToSource:
Closed. Six figures — spend against case, benefits by status, overdue reviews, top risks by exposure, gates due, exceptions open — every one of them assembled from the book with nothing typed, and every one able to say « not measured » with a reason. None carries a colour: no threshold for « too little benefit » has been agreed, and inventing one here is REQ-33 under a new name.

The figure we are most pleased with is the exceptions one, because it is a trap: a book with no tolerance set shows `—`, not « 0 open ». An empty exception register on a portfolio that has declared no limits is not a clean bill of health, and this is the only screen in the product that says so.

The snapshot extends `report_period` rather than inventing a second period. `report_snapshot` could not carry it — it is one row per project with fixed EV columns, and five of the six figures are portfolio aggregates with no project. Both new tables are append-only at the database, and the database itself refuses to store an unmeasured figure carrying a zero: `CHECK ((state = 'N' AND value IS NULL AND length(why) > 0) OR (state = 'measured' AND value IS NOT NULL))`. That constraint is REQ-33 written into the schema, and there is a test that inserts the forbidden row to prove the refusal.

Filing is refused if the period was closed on another day (409, naming both dates) and refused twice over (409, pointing at the restate path). Today's figures cannot be filed under March.

The caveat we gave you then — on a fresh book four of the six read as honest absences because the demonstration book carried no business case — is closed by REQ-48 in 5.24.0: the seed now carries business cases, some projects deliberately without one, and a fresh seed shows the six figures measured (server/test/demobook.test.js). What to try: seed a fresh book and open the value page.

Three of the four parts were already true and measured — the schema is published, `npm run review:field` never knew your name, and both gates hold EVERY register in docs/requests/ rather than the one we happen to have. channel.rule: issue #n = improvement I-n = REQ-0n; the Product Owner answers on the issue and closes it when the line is done
channel.counterpart: RT365 Program Orchestrator (docs/PMO.md); RT365 Product Owner agent decides on its side

acceptance.done: on the branch with its test
acceptance.accepted: the requester said so on the issue
acceptance.notAccepted: the requester is in a position to answer and has not — silence, or an objection not yet filed
acceptance.cannotAnswerYet: accepted is null: nothing is delivered to try, or the requester has said it cannot judge the line until it adopts the feature (E-9)

channel.escalation: a rejected refusal or done goes back to open with the objection quoted; the sponsor of both repositories is the tie-breaker

cadence.routine: Meridian Product Owner — RT365 field-return round
cadence.quietRound: a round that finds nothing new changes nothing and says so

release.state: 5.9.1 (PR #14) reached main on 23/09. The RT365 line (5.10.0–5.15.0) is merged onto it as 5.16.0 by docs/36 C-02, with one MER-04 rule (D-36.01) and one first-run implementation. Until the v5.16.0 tag is pushed, `released` stays false on every line.
release.consequence: 28 requests in this register read `done` or `partial`, and the files they name do not exist for anyone who clones. `released` is therefore false on every line, and honestly so.
release.gate: scripts/audit/register-reachable.mjs (F12) counts this on every `npm run audit` and fails a tag build that claims otherwise.
release.whatIsNeeded: A maintainer merges the branch to main and pushes the tag. The owner AUTHORISED the merge on 08/09; it was then refused by the agent session's own permission classifier — `git merge --ff-only`, `git push origin <branch>:main` and even a local `git tag -a` (D-33.50). Pushing a tag ref is separately refused HTTP 403 by the session credential (D-33.18, D-33.30). Two different boundaries, neither routed around.
